# Notes from a week without my phone

Last month I put my phone in a drawer for seven days. I didn't delete any apps or announce it on social media. I just told a few people how to reach me in an emergency, bought a cheap alarm clock, and closed the drawer.

## Day one

The first day was harder than I expected. I reached for my pocket at least thirty times before lunch. Every time I was waiting for something, the kettle, a bus, a friend running late, I felt a small jolt of panic at having nothing to look at.

## Days two and three

By the second day, the reaching had slowed down. I started noticing things I usually miss: the man who walks three greyhounds past my building every morning, the the smell of the bakery on the corner, the fact that my neighbor has been learning the trumpet.

I also noticed how often I use my phone to avoid being bored. Without it, boredom turned into something else. On the bus, I made a list of people I hadn't called in too long. In line at the grocery store, I worked out the plot of a short story I've been trying to write for a year.

## Days four and five

Practical problems started to show up. I missed a message about a change to a meeting time, and I had to call my bank from a payphone (they still exist, barely). Navigation was the hardest part. I printed directions to a friends house and still got lost.

These weren't disasters, but they were reminders of how much of my life depends on one device. It made me think about which uses I actually value and which ones are just habits.

## Days six and seven

By the end of the week, I felt calmer than I had in months. I was sleeping better, probably because I wasn't scrolling in bed. I read two books. I definately wasn't more productive at work, but I was less scattered.

## What I changed afterward

I didn't stay phone-free. That wasn't realistic, and I don't think it was the point. But I made a few changes that have stuck:

- The phone charges in the kitchen overnight.
- Social media apps live in a folder on the last screen.
- I leave the phone at home when I go for a walk.

None of this is new advice. You've probably read it all before. The difference for me was feeling, for a full week, what my attention was like without the constant pull. I hadn't realized how much I'd missed it.
